title: Mata Jito
hook: Guru Gobind Singh's wife, whom tradition credits with the sugar in the first amrit

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhangani, where Pir Budhu Shah rode in with his sons when the soldiers he vouched for walked away. Your line: a sufi's sacrifice.

An iron bowl. Clear water. A double-edged blade turning slowly through it, while hymns are recited over it, verse after verse. This is the scene Sikhs tell from the day the Khalsa was born at Anandpur: the Guru preparing amrit, the water of initiation. It's a scene of steel. Then, in the telling, someone steps forward with something small in her hands: sugar, little puffed sweets. She doesn't make a speech. She just drops them into the bowl. And the story says the Guru let them stay. Today: Mata Jito.
screen: `AN IRON BOWL, A DOUBLE-EDGED BLADE.` → `SOMEONE STEPS FORWARD.` → `SUGAR IN THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Mata Jito was a wife of Guru Gobind Singh. Mata means mother, a title of honor Sikhs use for the women of the Guru's household. Tradition remembers her as the mother of several of the Guru's sons, the ones Sikhs call the Sahibzade. Now, the bowl. Amrit is made with water and sugar puffs called patashas, stirred with a khanda, a double-edged sword, while sacred compositions are recited. The sugar is part of it to this day, and the story of how it got there is a story about a woman. The Guru was stirring the steel through the water. A wife of the Guru came and added the sweets. One telling says the Guru took it as a sign: the Khalsa would be brave, and it would also be sweet. Here the sources differ, and it's worth saying plainly. Some tellings, including the one this path follows today, give the sweets to Mata Jito. Others give the same moment to Mata Sahib Kaur, whom we meet in two days. Sikhs hold both tellings, and nobody needs to settle it to see the point. Steel alone can make someone hard. A sword can protect, but it can also make a person proud, quick, cold. The story puts sweetness in the same bowl, so whoever drinks it is meant to carry both: courage and gentleness, a straight back and a soft word. Sikhs speak of the ideal as saint and soldier together. This little story shows the saint half being stirred in, by a woman's hand, at the very bowl where the Khalsa began.
screen: `A WIFE OF GURU GOBIND SINGH.` · `WATER, STEEL AND SUGAR.` · `TWO TELLINGS, ONE MOMENT.` · `COURAGE AND GENTLENESS IN ONE BOWL.` · then, large: `SWEETNESS IN THE STEEL.`

segments.voice: Think of one place where you have to be strong right now: a hard conversation, a decision, someone you have to stand up to. Keep the strength, and picture sweetness in the same moment, a kinder first sentence, a pause before answering, a thank-you you'd usually skip. Hold both in the same bowl for a few breaths.
Mata Jito. A wife of Guru Gobind Singh, whom tradition credits with adding the sweets to the first amrit. Today's word.
Your line: sweetness in the steel. The sugar is still in the bowl. Day eight hundred eighteen, done.

chat.says: If amrit is stirred with a sword, why is there sugar in it?
options: One telling says the Guru took the sweets as a sign: the Khalsa would be brave and sweet.
It's there to make amrit a festive treat, so nobody takes the moment too seriously.
The sweets stand for the sword's victory, a reward for beating enemies in battle.

notes: Who added the patashas: the index credits Mata Jito; many tellings (and Sikh popular memory) credit Mata Sahib Kaur, and some historians hold Mata Jito died before the Khalsa's founding. The script states both tellings without deciding. A Keeper should decide whether this framing is right.
